## The question

<div class="question">Which cells contain this sequence?</div>

- A mutation
- A splice junction
- An unannotated RNA
- A microbial sequence

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 1 · <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10975-w">doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10975-w</a></div>

## What is lost in a gene-count matrix?

<div class="flow">
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Sequencing reads</b><small>ACGT… · cell barcode</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Reference mapping</b><small>assign reads to genes</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Cell × gene counts</b><small>many sequences, one gene total</small></div>
</div>

- Gene counts: a useful summary of expression
- Sequence differences: often absent from the summary
- Malva: query the underlying RNA sequence evidence

<div class="source">Paper, Introduction and Fig. 1</div>

## Glossary 1 · k-mers and probes

<div class="sequence-demo">
  <div><span class="label">Read</span><code>ACGTTACGAT</code></div>
  <div><span class="label">4-mers</span><code>ACGT</code> <code>CGTT</code> <code>GTTA</code> <code>TTAC</code> <code>TACG</code> <code>ACGA</code> <code>CGAT</code></div>
</div>

- **k-mer:** a sequence of *k* nucleotides
- **Probe:** sequence submitted for search
- **Index:** stored links between k-mers and their cells

<div class="aside">Illustration: overlapping 4-mers · Malva index: sampled 24-mers by default · probe search: sliding windows</div>

<div class="source">Paper, Methods: Malva Index architecture; sequence querying</div>

## Glossary 2 · interpretation

- **Reference / alternative allele:** two sequence forms at a variant site
- **Splice junction:** sequence joining two exons
- **Isoform:** one transcript form of a gene
- **Pseudocount:** Malva's k-mer match total; not a UMI count
- **Bucket:** group of related k-mers used as one cell feature

<div class="source">Paper, Figs. 3–5 and Discussion</div>

## Malva in one diagram

<div class="flow">
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Public FASTQ files</b><small>reads + cell barcodes</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Malva Index</b><small>k-mer → cells</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">←</div>
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Sequence query</b><small>variant · junction · gene</small></div>
</div>
<div class="resultbox">Matched cells + sample and cell metadata</div>

- Index each dataset; merge indices as data arrive
- Search across datasets without remapping reads

<div class="source">Paper, Fig. 1 and Methods</div>

## What is new here?

- Sequence search at **single-cell resolution** across a large public index
- Index design for low-memory queries and incremental updates
- Cell-by-sequence analysis beyond targeted searches

<div class="aside">Combined contribution: scalable retrieval · linked cell metadata · sequence-derived cell features</div>

<div class="source">Paper, Introduction, Figs. 1–2 and Fig. 5</div>

## How to read a positive result

<div class="threecol">
  <div><b>Probe</b><p>What sequence was searched?</p></div>
  <div><b>Observability</b><p>Was that locus sampled?</p></div>
  <div><b>Context</b><p>Which cell, donor, tissue and assay?</p></div>
</div>

- A hit: evidence for the queried RNA sequence
- No hit: may reflect limited expression or coverage
- Compare positive cells with a suitable denominator

<div class="source">Paper, Results and Limitations</div>

## 1 · Germline variation

<div class="question small">Can atlas RNA data recover known population variants?</div>

- 296,985 common, coding, biallelic SNPs
- 64-nucleotide allele-specific probes
- Healthy and disease samples; altered-sequence controls

<div class="source">Paper, Fig. 3b and “Screening for germline variation”</div>

## Germline screening · result and boundary

<div class="figure-split germline">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig3b.png" alt="Observed alternative allele frequencies in healthy and disease samples track population frequencies; altered-sequence controls do not."></figure>
<div class="figure-notes"><div class="takeaway">Observed allele frequencies tracked population expectations in healthy and disease samples.</div><p>The altered-sequence controls stayed near the background rate.</p><div class="boundary-note">A positive allele probe gives RNA sequence evidence. It does not resolve the donor genotype without coverage and allele-expression checks.</div></div>
</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 3b</div>

## 2 · Isoform usage

<div class="flow compact">
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Same gene</b><small>similar total counts</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">≠</div>
  <div class="flowbox"><b>Same transcript</b><small>different exons or 3′ ends</small></div>
</div>

- Probe a distinguishing exon, junction or 3′ UTR segment
- Compare signal across cell types or spatial regions
- Check assay coverage before interpretation

<div class="source">Paper, Fig. 3c–d</div>

## Example · <i>Ptprc</i> exon A

<div class="figure-split wide-figure">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig3c.png" alt="Coverage-like query across the Ptprc locus in Tabula Muris cell types."></figure>
<div class="figure-notes"><div class="takeaway">B cells show stronger inclusion of exon A than the other immune populations.</div><p>Gene totals conceal this exon-level contrast.</p><div class="boundary-note">Coverage supports exon usage. Full-length isoform assignment needs evidence across the transcript.</div></div>
</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 3c</div>

## Example · <i>Add2</i> 3′ UTR

<div class="figure-split add2">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig3d.png" alt="Add2 3-prime UTR coverage through mouse development and spatial maps of short and long forms."></figure>
<div class="figure-notes"><div class="takeaway">The distal 3′ UTR signal localises to developing neural tissue; the proximal form accumulates in liver.</div><p>Spatial context explains the apparent developmental shift in bulk profiles.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 3d</div>

## 3 · Cancer somatic mutations

<div class="question small">Can known tumour mutations be found in single-cell RNA?</div>

- Allele-specific probes for expressed SNVs
- Comparison with scTML mutation calls
- 280 tumour samples across 16 cancer types

<div class="source">Paper, Fig. 4 and “Querying cancer somatic mutations at scale”</div>

## Somatic mutations · what was shown

<figure class="paper-figure full-width">
  <img src="figs/fig4.png" alt="Pan-cancer mutation detection specificity and sensitivity, detection by mutation frequency, and sensitivity by mutation type.">
</figure>

<div class="result-line"><b>Across cancer types:</b> high specificity and mean sensitivity around 0.94. Splice-proximal variants were harder to recover.</div>

<div class="boundary-note compact-note">This benchmark tests retrieval of supplied mutations. Clone inference needs multiple informative loci and independent checks.</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 4a–c</div>

## 4 · From sequence search to cell comparison

<div class="figure-split representation">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig5a.png" alt="Sequenced cells represented as either cell-by-gene counts or cell-by-sequence features before dimensionality reduction."></figure>
<div class="figure-notes"><div class="takeaway">The same reads can support a gene-count representation or a sequence-derived representation.</div><p>Malva groups related k-mers into buckets, then builds an embedding for neighbours and clusters.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 5a; Methods: bucketing approach</div>

## Cell clustering from sequence composition

<div class="figure-grid clustering">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig5b.png" alt="Agreement between gene-count and sequence-based latent spaces across human tissues."><figcaption>Agreement varies by tissue and assay</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig5c.png" alt="Examples of low and high concordance between gene-based cell types and sequence-based clusters."><figcaption>Low and high clustering concordance</figcaption></figure>
</div>

<div class="boundary-note compact-note">Shared structure recovers familiar populations. Divergent clusters need biological evidence before interpretation.</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 5b–c and Extended Data Fig. 10</div>

## From a cluster to a marker sequence

<div class="figure-grid markers">
<figure class="paper-figure"><img src="figs/fig5e.png" alt="Gene-based and sequence-based spatial clusters in a head and neck tumour section."><figcaption>Sequence-derived clusters preserve tissue structure</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="paper-figure dark-panel"><img src="figs/fig5h.png" alt="Spatial expression of assembled marker sequences including short KLK10 and bacterial ribosomal RNA signals."><figcaption>Assembled markers localise within and outside the tissue</figcaption></figure>
</div>

<div class="result-line"><i>KLK10</i> short-form signal localised within tumour regions; bacterial rRNA markers appeared outside the tissue.</div>

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026, Fig. 5e,h</div>

## What can we do with the tool?

- **Targeted search:** a sequence → matching cells and samples
- **Coverage:** signal along a transcript or region
- **Cell representation:** buckets → clustering and markers

## Three possible research uses

<div class="threecol">
  <div><b>Data integration</b><p>Sequence features alongside gene counts; improvement on a defined task</p></div>
  <div><b>Lineage tracing</b><p>Mutation panel; combined evidence across loci and cells</p></div>
  <div><b>HCA survey</b><p>Clonal haematopoiesis variants in suitable public samples</p></div>
</div>

<div class="source">Discussion proposals; not applications validated in this paper</div>

## What must be checked?

- Locus coverage, transcript expression and 3′ capture bias
- Sequencing errors, probe specificity and related sequences
- Donor, study, assay and cell-type effects
- Independent evidence for genotype or clone assignment
- Privacy implications of donor-linked variants

<div class="source">Paper, Limitations and Supplementary Discussion</div>

## Discussion

- Which sequence questions are difficult with our current data?
- Where would a sequence layer add information to gene counts?
- What evidence would make a mutation-defined clone convincing?
- Is an HCA clonal haematopoiesis survey feasible with RNA coverage?

<div class="source">León-Periñán et al., <i>Nature</i> 2026</div>
